notes: Reported by the consumer-side validator during the round-9 live release of context r7livefull. Same class as backlog-cli-intent-hallucinated-anchor-045 and the backlog remedy fixes, now on the release-definition review path.
repro: Run release-definition with a live worker until a review REJECTS twice (budget spent), then read blocked.operator_command -> null
surface: dadaia lifecycle release-definition --harness codex (live review rejection)
symptom: On the live path, plan_review REJECTED the PLAN for a substantive reason and the run blocked with operator_command: null. The validator reported it could not proceed 'without inventing a change', which is exactly right: the operator is handed a rejection and no prescribed way forward. The workflow spends one bounded in-run revision of the create step and then returns the reviewer's RAW block unenriched, so the block carries whatever the reviewer produced — and a reviewer never fills operator_command. Every other gate in the engine prescribes its recovery; this one, the one a real release hits most often, does not.
title: A rejected review with the revision budget spent blocks with operator_command null — a dead end

evidence: Validator was right and it was a real dead end. RED first: tests/integration/cli/test_review_rejection_prescribes_recovery.py. Fix at root in the shared fragment gate, so it covers release-definition, audit and every future fragment workflow at once: when a review REJECTS and the one bounded in-run revision is already spent, the raw reviewer block is now enriched by prescribe_review_recovery() with the exact resume command - same run id, the create step that review consumes, the run's OWN harness - and the enriched block is persisted so the operator reads it from the ledger too. An operator_command a gate already set is never overwritten, so a more specific remedy still wins. Second defect found while fixing it: AgentRuntimeKind.CODEX_EXEC.value is 'codex_exec', which --harness REJECTS, so rendering the enum value into a command produced a line that fails the moment it is pasted - and my earlier backlog remedy fix had the same latent flaw for live runs. Both now render through HARNESS_CLI_NAMES, one canonical map in core that the CLI's own parser is derived from, with a test asserting every name it renders round-trips through _resolve_harness. GREEN: 2923 passed, ruff clean, mypy --strict clean.

expected: A BLOCKED run must not silently restart. Refuse it the way a COMPLETED re-run is refused, naming the recorded remedy and offering the two real choices: resume with --resume-from, or pass a fresh --run-id to start over deliberately.
notes: Reported during the round-10 live release of context r7livefull, and reproduced deterministically with --harness fake before fixing.
repro: Block a run, note blocked.operator_command, then re-run the identical command with the same --run-id and no --resume-from; the block is replaced by a fresh one from step 1
symptom: Re-invoking a workflow with the run id of a run that is BLOCKED, without --resume-from, does not resume and does not refuse: it starts the sequence over from the first step. The recorded block - its reason, its findings, and the operator_command that prescribes the recovery - is erased. Reproduced deterministically: a backlog-definition run blocked at backlog_review_gate with a remedy; re-running the identical command moved the block to backlog_author, destroying the original diagnosis. The consumer-side validator hit this on a LIVE release: the plan_review block vanished and the run restarted at spec_create. Re-running the same command is the most natural thing an operator does after a block, and it costs them the very information they need - and, on a live run, real worker spend.
title: Re-running a BLOCKED run with the same run id silently restarts it and destroys the block and its remedy

evidence: Reproduced deterministically before fixing: a backlog-definition run blocked at backlog_review_gate with a remedy; re-running the identical command moved the block to backlog_author, proving the restart had discarded the original diagnosis. Fix: refuse_blocked_restart() in the shared run_store guard, wired into all three engines (pipeline, fragment gate, backlog workflow) next to the existing completed-rerun guard, and applied ONLY on a fresh start — an explicit --resume-from is the sanctioned recovery and is never refused. The refusal hands over what the operator needs in one line: the step it blocked at, the recorded operator_command to resume with, the offer of a fresh --run-id to start over deliberately, and the reason. Verified on the real executed path: the re-run is refused with the full remedy and reason, and the prescribed resume then completes the run (exit 0). GREEN: 2924 passed, ruff clean, mypy --strict clean.

expected: The persisted mode matches what the operator asked for, or the command refuses.
notes: Reported during the round-10 live release attempt on context r7livefull.
repro: dadaia context bind <ctx> --mode spec --release <id>; read .dadaia/sessions/<sid>.json
symptom: Binding with '--mode spec' exited 0 reporting success, but the session record persisted mode READ rather than a spec/mutating mode.
title: context bind --mode spec persisted READ instead of the requested mode

reason: Working as designed, verified in the source and on the real executed path. 'spec' is a DOCUMENTED legacy alias of read: _BIND_MODE_ALIASES maps SPEC -> READ, the --mode help text says 'Legacy alias: spec maps to read', and the confirmation line the command printed said 'mode: read' — so the mapping was stated in the help, applied deterministically, and echoed back at the moment of binding. An unrecognized value is NOT silently degraded either: 'dadaia context bind <ctx> --mode nonsense' refuses with exit 1 naming the valid modes, which I re-ran to confirm. The valid mutating mode for lifecycle work is 'implementation', and binding with it persists BOUND_IMPLEMENTATION as expected. Rejecting rather than 'fixing' it because renaming or removing a documented alias would break operators who rely on it; the naming trap (spec SOUNDS like a phase, means read-only) is real but is a naming decision for the operator, not a defect to patch silently.

expected: An interrupted RUNNING run must tell the operator how to recover: resume from where it stopped, or take a fresh --run-id deliberately.
notes: Reported during round 11 while driving the full live cycle on context r11capture.
repro: Start a live release-definition, kill the driver mid-step, then inspect .dadaia/states/lifecycle/<run>.json (status running, blocked null) and re-run the same command
symptom: Interrupting release-definition leaves the Codex worker orphaned and the run persisted as 'running' at its current step: not finished, not failed, carrying no block and therefore no operator_command. The operator is left with a run that offers no guidance, and re-running the same command silently restarts from step one - redoing accepted live work at real cost.
title: An interrupted run is left RUNNING with no terminal state and no remedy

evidence: Fixed as the natural extension of the blocked-restart guard, since the recovery was always identical and nothing said so. refuse_blocked_restart now also covers RUNNING: re-invoking an interrupted run without --resume-from is refused with a line naming the step it stopped at, the exact resume command, and the fresh --run-id alternative. An explicit --resume-from is never refused. Verified on the real executed path: an interrupted run refuses with that guidance and the prescribed resume then completes it (exit 0) - which also confirms the earlier finding that a run left RUNNING by a dead driver was always resumable; what was missing was that nobody told the operator. GREEN: 2925 passed, ruff clean, mypy --strict clean.

expected: A re-executed create step must write a NEW attempt rather than mutating the attempt whose hash the ledger already recorded; and any handoff-immutability block must carry an operator_command, since no gate block may be a dead end.
notes: Found by driving the live release directly in the worker container, bypassing the Consumer task-runner window that had truncated every previous attempt. Evidence: <consumer-root>/workspace/.dadaia/states/lifecycle/r11-release-1.json on the validation host, wheel d0610d24 / commit 595a0e7b.
repro: Start a live release-definition, interrupt it after spec_review, resume with --resume-from plan_create, let plan_create+plan_review complete, and watch tasks_create block on the plan_create attempt-0 hash mismatch
symptom: Resuming a live release from plan_create advanced correctly through plan_create and plan_review, then BLOCKED at tasks_create with: 'required upstream handoff unavailable: step payload content hash mismatch for .../handoffs/r11-release-1/steps/plan_create-attempt-0.step-payload.json (payload was mutated - immutability violated)'. The ledger records spec_create, spec_review, plan_create, plan_review as accepted, so the work was done; the run still cannot advance because the plan_create payload on disk no longer hashes to what the ledger recorded. The block carries operator_command: null - another dead end, on the same run that the interrupted-run and rejected-review remedies were just added for. This is the release-definition-retry-collides-with-immutable-tasks-payload class resurfacing at a different step: a re-executed create step (resume, or the bounded in-run revision after a review rejection) writes over attempt-0 instead of recording a new attempt, so the immutable payload it already registered is mutated underneath the ledger.
title: A resumed create step rewrites attempt-0's payload, so the next step dies on an immutability violation with no remedy

reason: MY diagnosis was wrong; the engine is not at fault. I registered this CRITICAL after seeing tasks_create block on a plan_create attempt-0 hash mismatch. Checking the evidence instead of trusting my own reading: all four ledger hashes now match their files on disk byte for byte, and 'ps' showed FOUR dadaia/codex processes alive - Consumer' orphaned worker from the timed-out task was still running when I launched a detached resume on the SAME run id. Two executions writing one run's payload zone is what mutated it. Proof: once only ONE process remained, the same run re-ran plan_create, plan_review and tasks_create in sequence with no immutability error at all and advanced to tasks_implementability_review. So this is an operator-concurrency artifact I created, not a product defect. Rejecting rather than leaving a false CRITICAL on the ledger - the same discipline I apply to the validator's reports applies to mine. Worth noting for the future: concurrent runs on one run id are surfaced by no guard, but the NO-LOCKS doctrine accepts races by design, so that is a doctrine question for the operator, not a bug I should invent.

expected: release-definition accepts --demand exactly as backlog-definition does, injected into every executed model step's prompt, so an operator resuming after a rejection can supply the missing decision instead of re-rolling the same dice.
notes: Found while driving a live release to completion for the operator's readiness question. This is the difference between a recovery loop that converges because the operator can steer it, and one that only re-rolls.
repro: dadaia lifecycle release-definition --context <c> --release-id <r> --run-id <id> --harness codex --resume-from tasks_create --demand 'do X' -> 'No such option: --demand'
symptom: backlog-definition accepts --demand, which injects an '## Operator demand' block into every model step's prompt. release-definition does NOT: 'No such option: --demand'. So when a review REJECTS a SPEC, PLAN or TASKS, the operator's only channel back into the next attempt is the rejection digest the engine injects automatically - they cannot add the specific correction, constraint or decision the reviewer asked for. Observed on the live path across three rejection cycles of one release: the reviewer moved from a pytest cache-flag lint, to unresolved toolchain markers, to 'the draft leaves essential construction, serialization and storage-mapping decisions to the implementer'. The model IS converging, but each cycle costs minutes of live worker time and the operator has to sit and hope rather than say the one sentence that would resolve it.
title: release-definition has no --demand, so an operator cannot inject the correction a review asked for

evidence: Fixed in the shared fragment gate, so release-definition and audit both gain it rather than release-definition alone: when an operator demand is present it is injected into EVERY executed model step as an '## Operator demand' block, the same shape backlog-definition has carried since backlog-define-has-no-demand-input-channel. release-definition's run() accepts operator_demand and the CLI exposes --demand with help that names its purpose: the channel for supplying the decision a review asked for when resuming after a REJECTED verdict. Verified: the flag renders in --help, the workflow signature accepts it, and the gate injects it. GREEN: 2928 passed, ruff clean, mypy --strict clean.

expected: Either the review converges on a TASKS draft the author can realistically produce, or the gate bounds the loop and tells the operator the bar it is holding and what would satisfy it. A reviewer that restates the same objection without narrowing is not reviewable work - the author cannot act on it, and the operator cannot either.
notes: Observed while driving the live cycle for an operator readiness question, on wheel 14a5611c with the new --demand channel in place. This is the reason a live release has never been witnessed reaching completed with consumed_backlog.json: not an engine defect - every gate, remedy and ledger behaved correctly throughout - but a prompt-contract mismatch between what tasks-create can produce and what tasks-review-implementability demands.
repro: Author three real backlog items live, run release-definition --harness codex, and resume tasks_create after each rejection, including with --demand supplying the exact specificity the reviewer asks for
symptom: On a real three-item data-capture release (context r11capture, v0.11.0), tasks_implementability_review REJECTED five consecutive tasks_create attempts and never approved. The first cycles narrowed usefully - a pytest cache-flag lint, then unresolved toolchain markers, then 'leaves construction, serialization, storage-mapping decisions to the implementer', then 'task boundaries still require an implementer to invent interfaces, payload shapes, or prerequisite code'. The fifth, after an operator demand that explicitly required per-task file paths, exact public signatures with parameter and return types, field-by-field payload shapes, inter-task dependencies by id, and a decision for every open design point, came back as 'As tarefas ainda exigem decisoes de implementacao nao especificadas' - shorter and vaguer than its predecessor, i.e. restating rather than narrowing. The upstream SPEC and PLAN were both APPROVED by the same reviewer family, so the release is not blocked on scope quality. Consequence: a real release-definition can stall indefinitely at this gate, burning roughly ten minutes of live worker time per cycle, with no mechanism that ends the loop.
title: tasks_implementability_review rejects indefinitely on a realistic release, even with explicit operator steering

expected: plan_review must REJECT a PLAN that omits a contract binding for any new or changed caller-facing surface, so the omission is fixed where it is fixable. A downstream gate must never be the first place an upstream omission is detected, when the downstream step is forbidden from repairing it.
notes: Diagnosed by reading the three fragments against each other rather than by another live cycle. The fix belongs in plan-review's checklist and needs its own verification round; deliberately NOT attempted here, because a wrong change to a review contract is worse than a documented gap.
repro: Run release-definition live; when tasks_implementability_review rejects repeatedly for unspecified implementation decisions, read the approved PLAN and check whether it carries exact signatures, field types and module paths for each caller-facing surface
surface: dadaia lifecycle release-definition --harness codex (plan_review then tasks_implementability_review)
symptom: This is the ROOT CAUSE of tasks-implementability-review-does-not-converge-on-a-real-release, found by diffing the three fragments against each other. plan-create.md REQUIRES, for every new or changed caller-facing surface, an explicit contract binding - exact public type/function/method names, parameter and return signatures, field names/types, module/export path - and says in as many words 'do not leave them for TASKS or implementation to invent'. tasks-create.md then FORBIDS the author from supplying what the PLAN omitted: it must copy the bindings 'already approved in the PLAN' and 'never invent a binding missing from the approved PLAN'. tasks-review-implementability.md REQUIRES those same bindings to be present. So when plan_review approves a PLAN that lacks them, the TASKS author is trapped between two rules it cannot both satisfy, and the rejection lands at tasks_implementability_review - one step downstream of where the omission actually happened, and at the one step that cannot repair it. Observed live: five consecutive TASKS rejections that stopped narrowing and began restating, on a release whose PLAN had been APPROVED.
title: plan_review approves a PLAN without contract bindings, trapping tasks_create in an unsatisfiable gate

evidence: Fixed where the omission is repairable: plan-review.md's architecture checklist gains a 'Contract bindings present' row requiring, for every NEW or CHANGED caller-facing surface, the exact public name, parameter and return signature, field names and types, and module/export path — and REJECTING a PLAN that leaves any of them to TASKS or implementation. The row states WHY it is not a style note: tasks-create is forbidden to invent a binding the PLAN omitted while tasks-review-implementability requires it present, so an approved-but-unbound PLAN traps the TASKS author between two rules and the failure surfaces at the one step that cannot repair it. Pinned by a contract test asserting plan-create still demands the bindings AND plan-review now checks them, so the pair cannot drift apart again. The release_definition golden was regenerated; its diff is exactly this one row. GREEN: 2929 passed, ruff clean, mypy --strict clean.

The premise of my own report was wrong once the root cause was fixed: the loop DOES converge, and it was the missing plan_review contract-binding check that made it look otherwise. Before the fix the TASKS author was forbidden to invent bindings the PLAN omitted while its reviewer required them - an unsatisfiable pair, which is why five cycles stopped narrowing and began restating. After adding the plan_review check and steering the PLAN through --demand: plan_review APPROVED the rebuilt PLAN with full bindings, and the TASKS verdicts then narrowed monotonically - from 'tasks still require unspecified implementation decisions' (vague, unactionable) to 'still leaves cursor contracts, record deserialization and CLI composition' (three named gaps) to 'T7 does not bind the concrete runtime collaborators needed to construct any CLI flow' (ONE task, ONE gap). Each rejection was substantive, actionable, and answerable through the --demand channel. What remains is iteration count on a genuinely demanding reviewer, not a gate that cannot be satisfied. Recording this rather than leaving a false 'does not converge' on the ledger: the original title describes the symptom of plan-review-approves-a-plan-missing-its-contract-bindings, which is fixed and tested.

expected: The scaffold commit stages only the specs/ baseline it authors. Pre-existing unrelated worktree modifications are left untouched and uncommitted, per the workspace rule that a commit stages exactly what its change touched and never uses -A over a shared tree.
notes: Found while replicating a workspace onto a second machine: the destination repo came back clean with an extra commit, which initially read as data loss until the scaffold commit was inspected. No data was lost, but the operator's WIP was committed without consent and the commit message misdescribes its contents.
repro: 1. In a workspace, take a context repo and modify two tracked files unrelated to specs (leave them uncommitted). 2. Run 'dadaia context alive <ctx>'. 3. git show --stat HEAD: the scaffold commit includes the two unrelated files; git status is now clean.
symptom: Running 'dadaia context alive <ctx>' on a context whose repo has a dirty working tree produces a commit titled 'chore(scaffold): dadaia context alive specs baseline' that contains, besides the specs/ scaffold, every unrelated modified tracked file present in the worktree (observed: a compose file and a supervisor config), silently authoring the operator's in-progress work into a commit they did not intend.
title: dadaia context alive commits pre-existing unrelated worktree changes into its scaffold commit

expected: ensure_workspace_venv pins the child venv to an interpreter satisfying the package's requires-python (e.g. honor pyvenv.cfg 'executable', validate the created venv's version, or search for a satisfying python3.X) instead of inheriting implicit base-executable resolution; failure message should name the interpreter mismatch cause, not only the index/wheel fallback.
notes: Environment-sensitive and CI-blind: green in CI where python3>=3.12; breaks the documented self-hosting/consumer setup on Ubuntu 22.04 (§6: a green internal gate that diverges from real consumer behavior is itself a bug). Found during v0.8.0 milestone-a local test run.
repro: 1. On a host whose default python3 is <3.12 but which has python3.12 available, create a venv: python3.12 -m venv --copies <venv>. 2. Install dadaia-workspace into it. 3. Run <venv>/bin/dadaia init -w <fresh-dir>. 4. Bootstrap creates the child venv via stdlib venv.create(), which inherits the degraded base (python3), and the editable/package install fails the requires-python check. Deterministic; also reproduced by the e2e test test_full_handoff_emit_and_validate on such a host. A venv created WITHOUT --copies (symlinks) resolves base to python3.12 and the same flow succeeds.
symptom: Running 'dadaia init' from a Python installed in a venv created with --copies produces a child workspace venv on the interpreter that sys._base_executable degrades to (the unversioned python3 of the venv home), not the interpreter recorded in pyvenv.cfg 'executable'. On hosts where python3 predates 3.12 the subsequent package install fails with 'requires a different Python: 3.10.x not in >=3.12' and init exits 1.
title: dadaia init creates a workspace venv violating its own requires-python when run from a --copies venv

evidence: Reproduced on the exact executed path pre-fix: tests/e2e/features/test_handoff_pipeline.py::test_full_handoff_emit_and_validate FAILED with 'requires a different Python: 3.10.12 not in <4.0,>=3.12' (dadaia init exit 1) on this host (--copies venv, sys._base_executable degrades to /usr/bin/python3->3.10). RED unit repro added: tests/unit/infrastructure/test_python_env.py::test_resolve_child_venv_interpreter_skips_degraded_base_and_uses_pyvenv_executable and 11 sibling tests (12 failed/errored pre-fix, captured). Root-cause fix in dadaia_workspace/infrastructure/python_env.py: ensure_workspace_venv resolves+verifies an explicit interpreter (sys._base_executable if it satisfies Requires-Python, else the running venv's own pyvenv.cfg 'executable', else a version-pinned pythonX.Y on PATH) and creates the child venv via subprocess 'python -m venv --copies' instead of implicit venv.create(); a pre-install post-condition (_assert_child_interpreter_version) now names an interpreter mismatch explicitly before ever reaching pip's bare error, covering both surfaces named (dadaia init / workspace venv bootstrap). GREEN post-fix: same e2e test passes (9.13s); full suite 2135 passed, 3 skipped, 0 failed (-p no:cacheprovider); ruff format --check, ruff check, mypy --strict all clean on touched files. Shipped as hotfix/v0.5.1 merged into develop at 6df671b9, pyproject.toml 0.5.0->0.5.1, CHANGELOG.md [0.5.1] entry added.

expected: No .mypy_cache/ directory materializes in the repo working tree when running the documented local command with no extra env var.
notes: CI already works around this correctly via MYPY_CACHE_DIR=$RUNNER_TEMP/mypy (ci.yml:119-120) but the pyproject.toml comment and the plain local invocation documented for agents ('mypy --strict dadaia_workspace/') do not carry that redirect, so a direct local run pollutes the repo root (tests/conftest.py's session-pollution guard correctly flags it). Workaround used this session: MYPY_CACHE_DIR=<tmp-dir> mypy --strict dadaia_workspace/. Root cause is likely a mypy 2.x behavior change where incremental=false no longer suppresses cache_dir writes by itself; either set cache_dir explicitly to a path outside the repo in pyproject.toml, or document the MYPY_CACHE_DIR requirement for local invocations.
repro: cd repos/dadaia-workspace; rm -rf .mypy_cache; .dadaia/.venv/bin/mypy --strict dadaia_workspace/; ls .mypy_cache (directory exists).
symptom: pyproject.toml's [tool.mypy] comment states 'incremental = false already disables the mypy cache, so no .mypy_cache/ is created in the repo tree' - false in practice.
title: mypy --strict dadaia_workspace/ creates .mypy_cache/ at repo root despite incremental=false

expected: The product has a sanctioned way to publish its own positive privacy fixtures. The self-scan sentinel already reconciles this tension with a shrink-only _TESTS_SCOPE_BASELINE of deliberate synthetic fixture literals; the push gate has no equivalent notion, so the two enforcement surfaces disagree about the same files. Either the push scan recognises the same declared synthetic-fixture rows, or fixtures are expressed so no contiguous matching literal reaches a blob (the pattern the sentinel module itself already uses for its own archive fixture, composing the literal at runtime).
notes: Found by the security-reviewer running the real chokepoint for the v0.4.2 ship review (milestone b). The values involved are synthetic and non-identifying, so there is no privacy exposure - the defect is that the gate and the release law are mutually unsatisfiable: SPEC/PLAN/TASKS for the release all state 'No --no-verify, ever', and --no-verify is the only remaining push path. The release CLOSURE records this evidence row as 'Milestone (b) pending T-042-21', so it was never observed before now. Amnesty behaviour itself is correct and was verified separately: 24 of 31 structural hits in the range are correctly suppressed as already published at the same path.
repro: On a branch that adds a new baseline pattern plus its positive fixture, feed the real pre-push stdin line (<local-ref> <local-sha> <remote-ref> <remote-sha>) to 'dadaia ci push-gate-check'. The scan blocks with 'the pushed range publishes N object(s) carrying a denylisted term', naming the fixture paths and the new pattern id as the source layer.
surface: pre-push chokepoint (push-range denylist scan) vs privacy-baseline positive fixtures
symptom: A release that adds a POSITIVE fixture for a new privacy-baseline pattern cannot push it. The fixture must carry a value the pattern matches (that is what makes it a positive), the fixture file is a NEW blob at a NEW path so the prior-published-term amnesty grants it nothing, and the push-range scan therefore refuses the ref. Running the real chokepoint over the v0.4.2 ship range refuses six objects: the two new fixture files and the test module that inlines the same expected fragment.
title: The push-range denylist scan refuses the release's own positive privacy-baseline fixtures, leaving no sanctioned push path

expected: A document that merely names the no-reply address the law mandates in every commit trailer is not a privacy leak and must not be refused. Either the carve-out covers the local-part form (with a counter-fixture proving a genuine mailbox at the same apex domain still fires), or the release documents express the address so no contiguous matching literal reaches a blob - the precedent the product already uses for its own fixtures.
notes: Found by the security-reviewer running the real chokepoint for the v0.4.3 milestone-a definition push. No privacy exposure: the address is a public vendor no-reply mailbox already published unmasked in thousands of this repo's commit trailers. surface: pre-push chokepoint (push-range denylist scan) vs the packaged privacy baseline's email-address carve-out
symptom: The baseline's email-address exclude_regex is domain-anchored: it carves out the vendor's dotted no-reply subdomain and the GitHub no-reply subdomain, but not the plain vendor domain used by the co-author trailer DADAIA.md itself mandates (local part 'noreply', vendor apex domain). Any TRACKED BLOB that writes that address contiguously is therefore refused by the push-range denylist scan, while the sdd-gate-v3 memory atom advertises 'the noreply mail domains' as carved out. Commit messages are unaffected today because the scan reads blobs only.

expected: An error present before the migration stays classified as pre-existing regardless of how many other atoms the migration repaired - the fail-and-restore path is reserved for regressions the migration itself introduced. Comparison should be per-atom/per-finding identity rather than the aggregated description string.
notes: Found during the pre-push security review of the 0.4.3 develop delta while probing whether the new link-refusal and skip-on-unreadable guards trade a security bug for a stuck upgrade. The guards themselves behave correctly - the link target is left untouched and healthy atoms still migrate; only the post-run classification is wrong. Not a security finding: no confidentiality or integrity boundary is crossed, and the tree is recoverable. Reproduced on throwaway trees under the agent scratch area; no repository file was modified.
repro: 1. Scaffold a specs tree, regress its constitution stamp to pattern version 1, and give three memory atoms the retired keys agent_tier and token_estimate. 2. Add a fourth atom as a SYMLINK whose target lives outside the specs tree and also carries a retired key. 3. Run 'dadaia specs upgrade --specs-dir <tree> -y'. Observed: the three real atoms migrate, the symlinked one is correctly refused by the link guard, and the command exits 1 with 'upgrade introduced 1 new doctor error(s). Restore from: <backup>' naming the symlinked atom. Control: repeat with the symlinked atom as the ONLY violator (no other retired keys anywhere) and the same tree reports '[warn] ... 1 pre-existing doctor error(s) remain (not caused by the upgrade) - fix separately, do NOT restore' and exits 0. The only difference is whether the aggregated description changed.
symptom: The pre/post doctor comparison keys on the tuple (code, description), but LINT-1 aggregates EVERY violating memory atom into one issue whose description lists them all. When a migration fixes some violating atoms and legitimately skips another (a symlinked atom under the new link-refusal guard, or an unreadable/unwritable one under the new skip paths), the LINT-1 description shrinks, no longer matches the pre-migration snapshot, and the residual violation is misclassified as newly introduced. The command then prints 'upgrade introduced 1 new doctor error(s). Restore from: <backup>' and exits 1 even though the tree reached the target pattern version cleanly and the surviving violation predates the run. Following that instruction discards a good version bump while leaving the same error in place - exactly the harm the code's own comment says the comparison exists to prevent.
title: specs upgrade reports a pre-existing LINT-1 as newly introduced whenever a migration legitimately skips one atom

expected: A fixture aged for a test that injects a clock is aged by THAT clock, so the test asserts the same thing on every calendar day. A test whose result depends on the wall-clock date is a time bomb, not a test.
notes: Pre-existing; surfaced by a push that happened to land after midnight UTC. Discovered while chasing a CI failure that looked like a regression but was not.
repro: 1. Run the tmp_gc suite while the real UTC date equals 2026-08-18 — green. 2. Run the identical commit after 00:00Z on 2026-08-19 — four tests fail on marker-age assertions. No code change in between.
symptom: run_tmp_gc takes an injectable now and the tests pass a frozen _NOW = 2026-08-18T00:00Z, but the fixture helpers age files with time.time() (the real clock): _write_marker at line 49, and raw os.utime aging at lines 109 and 318. The service therefore measures a real-clock mtime against a frozen now, so the effective age drifts by exactly the distance between the two. A marker written as '4 days old' had only about 0.04 days of margin over the 3-day threshold. When real UTC crossed midnight into 2026-08-19 the age fell to 2.99 days and four tests began failing: test_orphan_marker_older_than_three_days_reaped, test_dry_run_reports_all_lanes_without_deleting_anything, test_idempotent_second_real_run_is_a_pure_no_op, test_unlink_failure_is_best_effort_and_does_not_abort_other_lanes. The same suite passed 30 minutes earlier on the same commit and the same machine; CI went red on Linux, macOS and Windows simultaneously.
title: tmp_gc tests age fixtures with the real clock while injecting a frozen now — the suite breaks at a UTC date boundary

evidence: REPRO (executed path, no code change involved): the tmp_gc suite passed at 2026-08-18T23:3xZ (full suite 2614 passed) and four of its tests failed at 2026-08-19T00:09Z on the same commit and machine — test_orphan_marker_older_than_three_days_reaped, test_dry_run_reports_all_lanes_without_deleting_anything, test_idempotent_second_real_run_is_a_pure_no_op, test_unlink_failure_is_best_effort_and_does_not_abort_other_lanes. CI went red on Linux, macOS and Windows in the same run. ROOT CAUSE: run_tmp_gc receives an injectable clock and the tests inject a frozen _NOW of 2026-08-18T00:00Z, but the fixtures were aged with time.time() — the real clock — at three sites (the _write_marker helper plus two raw os.utime calls). The service therefore compared a real-clock mtime against a frozen now, so the effective age drifted by the distance between the two clocks; a marker written as 4 days old carried only ~0.04 days of margin over the 3-day threshold and fell to 2.99 days the moment real UTC crossed midnight. FIX: all three sites now derive the mtime from _NOW.timestamp(), the same clock the service is given, so the assertions hold on every calendar day rather than only on the day the tests were authored. GREEN: tmp_gc suite 17 passed; full suite 2614 passed, 3 skipped; ruff format, ruff check clean.

expected: A test asserts the CONTRACT, not a platform-specific value: capture the mode on disk before the operation and assert it is unchanged. That holds on every platform and is what mode preservation means.
notes: Authored during this mint in response to a security finding about mkstemp's 0600 leaking onto the target; the production fix was correct, the test was not portable. Same class as the GC-suite Windows fixture bug this repo already hit.
repro: 1. Run the mode-preservation test on a Windows runner. 2. It fails with assert 438 == 420 (0o666 vs 0o644) even though the code under test is correct.
symptom: The test guarding that an atomic repair does not narrow a file's mode asserted a literal 0o644. Windows has no POSIX mode bits — chmod only toggles the read-only attribute and every file reads back 0o666 — so it failed with 'assert 438 == 420' on both Windows jobs while every Linux and macOS job passed. The local gate and five security-review passes all run on Linux and none could surface it; only the multi-platform CI did.
title: The mode-preservation test hard-coded 0o644, which no Windows runner can satisfy

evidence: REPRO: CI run on the pushed tip failed both Windows jobs with 'assert 438 == 420' at test_repair_preserves_file_mode_and_newlines, while all Linux and macOS jobs passed. ROOT CAUSE: the assertion pinned a literal 0o644, a value Windows cannot produce because it has no POSIX mode bits. FIX: capture stat.S_IMODE before the migration and assert equality after, so the test states the contract (the repair does not change the mode) rather than a umask-specific value. GREEN locally: the file's 10 tests pass and the full suite is 2614 passed, 3 skipped; the real verification is the CI run on the next push, where the Windows jobs must go green.

expected: A fixture that exists to prove line-ending behaviour is written with explicit newline= so its own bytes are known on every platform, and the assertion can only fail for the reason it names.
notes: Same family as the mode literal that just turned Windows red — a test whose truth depends on the platform rather than on the contract. Currently passing, so latent rather than active.
repro: On a Windows runner, make the fixture carry no retired key (or place it where a guard skips it): the assertion fails although the repair behaved correctly.
symptom: The fixture for the newline test is written with write_text and no newline=argument, so on Windows it lands as CRLF. The assertion that the repaired file contains no CRLF then holds only because the migration rewrote the file. Should the fixture ever stop carrying a retired key, or be skipped by one of the new guards, the assertion flips to a Windows-only failure that blames the repair for the fixture's own line endings.
title: A CRLF-carrying fixture makes the newline assertion pass for the wrong reason on Windows

expected: Either the behaviour is stated — LF-canonical output, consistent with the projection contract — or the module stops claiming it byte-preserves everything outside the removed keys. Right now the docstring and the behaviour disagree.
notes: Pre-existing composition of two correct decisions, not introduced by this mint. Probably desirable as behaviour; the defect is the wording, and a test either way would pin whichever is chosen.
repro: Write a memory atom with CRLF endings and a retired frontmatter key, run the migration, and compare the raw bytes before and after: every line ending changed.
symptom: read_text applies universal-newline translation on the way in and the writer passes newline= on the way out, so an atom that arrives with CRLF endings leaves with LF on every line — not only the ones touched. Reproduced on Linux, since universal-newline reading is cross-platform. An atom carrying no retired key keeps its CRLF, so the normalisation applies only to migrated files. No test detects it, because both sides of every comparison normalise.
title: Migrating a CRLF atom rewrites every line ending to LF, which the byte-preserve wording does not admit

expected:
A linter on SDD markdown may normalize whitespace/formatting only. It MUST
NOT mutate `[ ] / [-] / [x]` task markers (a grep-parsable machine contract,
`dadaia-task-manager` skill), MUST NOT change `**Status:**` tokens
(`Draft`/`Em revisão`/`Aprovado` are author-controlled SDD gate tokens), and MUST NOT
inject or duplicate body content. These are semantic SDD state, not formatting.
notes:
re-filed from a consumer context ledger 2026-08-23 (misfiled; audit SDD-27). Original notes: Task-marker integrity is the basis of the implement→review→DONE protocol; a
linter flipping markers silently corrupts traceability and the gate's implicit contract.
The authoring agent had to fully rewrite `TASKS.md` to restore the correct all-`[ ]`
state. No operator-local paths/secrets involved. Root cause likely a markdown formatter
hooked on file write that treats list-item checkbox state and frontmatter-like headers as
reformattable. Fix: exclude `specs/releases/**/{SPEC,PLAN,TASKS,CLOSURE}.md` task markers
+ `**Status:**` lines from any auto-formatter, or disable content-mutating linting on
`specs/**` markdown entirely.
repro:
```
# In a DEFINITION-phase release dir:
1. Write specs/releases/<id>/TASKS.md with all tasks `[ ]` and Status: Em revisão.
2. Apply a small Edit to an unrelated line.
3. Re-read the file: a task marker has been changed to [-]/[x], and/or
   the Status header has been flipped, and/or a duplicate paragraph appended.
```
surface: SDD artifact post-write linter (editing specs/releases/<id>/{SPEC,PLAN,TASKS}.md via file tools)
symptom:
While authoring/revising the v0.4.0 release artifacts in
`specs/releases/v0.4.0/`, a post-write linter mutated the markdown between an Edit's
`Read` and its `old_string` apply — repeatedly forcing "File has been modified since
read" errors. Worse, the linter made **semantic** changes to load-bearing content, not
just whitespace normalization:

1. **Flipped a task marker** in `TASKS.md` from `[ ]` (OPEN) to `[-]` and then to `[x]`
   (DONE) on `T-A.1` — a task that has NOT been implemented (the release is in DEFINITION
   phase, no `[-]` reservation, no commit). A false `[x]` is a machine-contract lie that
   would let an implementer skip the work and a closure to proceed on unbuilt scope.
2. **Injected a duplicate, contradictory block** into `PLAN.md` — a second
   "Mid-sequence partial-apply recovery" paragraph that reintroduced a per-stack manual
   ordering narrative the spec review had explicitly corrected (ordering safety is a
   merged-commit property, not a run sequence).
3. **Flipped `**Status:** Em revisão` → `Aprovado`** on SPEC/PLAN/TASKS during editing,
   independent of the authoring agent's explicit status-flip step.
title: sdd-artifact-linter-mutates-task-markers
